Survey Methodologist · Quantitative Researcher

Jiayun Jin

My work begins with a single question: are we observing what we think we are observing? Between a survey response and the attitude it claims to capture, between a sample and the population it is meant to represent, between a coded answer and the meaning it is assumed to carry — something always intervenes. I study that something.

One continuous question, moving across measurement, inference, and interpretation.

01 / About

I am a quantitative researcher specialising in survey methodology and measurement. My work focuses on what stands between a question and the construct it is meant to capture — how instruments are designed, where data quality breaks down, and what assumptions link observed numbers to what they are meant to represent.

I was trained in statistical monitoring and survey data quality at KU Leuven. My doctoral work examined how survey data collection can be monitored for signs of measurement error and later received the Innovation Prize at the Netherlands Platform for Survey Research. Since then, I have extended the same measurement questions into non-probability survey inference and transparent coding of open-ended responses. The data settings change; the question stays the same.

I am currently based in the Netherlands, developing these projects and interested in applied research settings where measurement rigour and practical impact need to work together.

02 / Research

Research Areas

My work connects survey methodology, measurement quality, and computational workflows — asking how we can build reliable indicators and transparent analytical systems for complex social data.

Survey Measurement & Data Quality

Questionnaire-based measurement, response quality assessment, measurement error, and the interpretation of survey indicators in large-scale data collection.

Survey Inference & Adjustment

Simulation-based evaluation of calibration weighting, inverse probability weighting, mass imputation, and doubly robust methods for non-probability survey samples.

Open-Ended Responses & Text Coding

Transparent workflows for coding open-ended survey responses, with attention to reliability, uncertainty, and interpretability in model-assisted coding.

Latent Structure & Heterogeneity

Mixture models, latent-class analysis, and structured heterogeneity detection in attitudinal and behavioral data.

Social Inequality & Attitudes

Gender attitudes, hidden patterns in attitudinal surveys, and the relationship between observed responses and underlying constructs.

Open & Reproducible Workflows

Building research tools that make data processing, analytical assumptions, and measurement decisions auditable, shareable, and reproducible.

Software & Research Projects

Non-Probability Survey Inference

R simulation workflow for survey inference under selection bias
View on GitHub ↗

An R-based methodological project comparing calibration weighting, inverse probability weighting, mass imputation, and doubly robust estimation under different selection mechanisms and auxiliary-information conditions. The project asks a conditional question rather than seeking a single “best” method: when do adjustment methods work, and when do their assumptions break down?

✓ Works well

Takeaway: there is no universally best method — performance depends on the selection mechanism and the quality of auxiliary information.
Beyond binary: a continuous non-ignorability gradient
A follow-up round replaces the binary ignorable / non-ignorable comparison with a continuous parameter (γ) controlling how strongly selection depends on the outcome. Once γ > 0, calibration, IPW, and doubly robust estimation become close substitutes — their differences are small relative to the bias γ introduces. What matters is whether the auxiliary variables can proxy for that outcome-dependence: strong auxiliary information absorbs part of the bias, while weak auxiliary information offers little protection.
See preliminary results (γ-sweep chart)

LISS Panel Quality & Representativeness

Reproducible monitoring of panel composition and participation
View on GitHub ↗
R Panel Representativeness Data Quality Audit Longitudinal Monitoring
What it does

A reproducible monitoring workflow for the LISS panel (Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences), built on the monthly LISS Background Variables. Audits the underlying monthly files for schema and data-quality consistency across waves, and compares the panel's age and sex composition against CBS population benchmarks — separately for the full eligible panel and for participating members.

Early-stage: the background-file audit and representativeness monitoring are implemented; participation/attrition monitoring and a weighting demonstration linked to nonprob-survey-inference are planned next.
Age representation vs. CBS benchmark
Younger age groups (16–24, 25–34) are underrepresented, and the gap widens further among participating members; older groups (55+) are overrepresented, most sharply at 65+.
See more (panel size over time)
Panel size over time
Both the full eligible panel and the participating subset have shrunk over the 27 monthly waves, with the participating panel declining somewhat faster — an early look at the attrition question the in-progress participation-monitoring work is meant to answer directly.
Active Development

OpenCodebook

A Python framework for transparent, auditable, model-assisted coding of open-ended survey responses. Researchers define structured codebooks in YAML; local open-source models apply the codes; the pipeline produces structured outputs with reliability diagnostics and reviewable audit trails. The project extends my survey-measurement work into open-ended text, asking how qualitative responses can be coded at scale without losing interpretability.

Gender Attitude Latent Structures

Research on hidden heterogeneity in gender attitude surveys using mixture models and latent-class analysis. Published in Sociological Methods & Research (2025). Currently extending to open-ended text responses.

Fig. 1 — A response-process model for Likert-scale answers
Fig. 4 — Latent profile membership by gender and education
From Jin (2025), Disentangling and Reassembling: Unveiling Hidden Patterns in Gender Attitudinal Surveys, Sociological Methods & Research. A multi-process response model separates non-substantive, midpoint, and extreme response tendencies from underlying gender attitudes, identifying five latent profiles whose prevalence varies systematically by gender and education.
